lessons.title: Web Applications: JavaScript and the DOM

notes.summary: CS142 is the payoff course: build real web applications with JavaScript, React, Node, and databases — the full architecture you've been using all along in Full Stack Ocean. This first unit is deep JavaScript: closures, prototypes, async, and the DOM. Your CS50 week 8 was the preview; this is the professional version.
notes.focus: Rewrite one CS50 week-8 exercise with modern JS (arrow functions, modules, fetch). Feeling the language's real expressiveness sets the term's tone.

notes.summary: Component architecture: props down, events up, state as the minimal mutable core, and the render cycle as a function of state. You study React's model (hooks, keys, lifting state) and the design judgment of decomposition. Full Stack Ocean's own frontend is React — study its source as a living lab.
notes.focus: Read Full Stack Ocean's Study.js (or Jobs.js) and diagram its component tree: state ownership, props flow, and event direction. A real app as a case study.

notes.summary: JavaScript on the server: Node's event loop (single-threaded async I/O — your 6.829 queueing intuition applies), Express-style routing, middleware as function composition, and REST API design. This is the exact stack of this app's backend (Express + routes + middleware) — you can read the production code you use.
concepts: Async I/O and callbacks to promises
notes.focus: Read this app's server.js and one route file (jobs.js). Every concept in this lesson is IN THERE — recognize the patterns in production code.

notes.summary: 6.830's theory meets the web: schemas for application data, ORMs vs raw queries, transactions around multi-step operations, and indexes for query performance. Connection pooling and N+1 query pitfalls — the practical layer your database course deliberately left as an exercise.
notes.focus: Design the schema for an app you'd like to build, then write the three most important queries by hand. Own the SQL even if an ORM writes it.

notes.summary: The web's identity layer: password storage (hash and salt — never plaintext), session cookies vs JWTs, OAuth delegation, and the CSRF/XSS defenses from 6.858 applied as CODE. Implementing login end to end (including the failure paths) is the assignment — and the most security-relevant code you'll ever ship.
notes.focus: Audit the login flow of an app you built against 6.858's checklist. Finding one real hardening gap (timing, token entropy, cookie flags) makes the audit real.

lessons.title: Asynchronous Clients: fetch, Promises, and State

notes.summary: The network in the UI: fetching from APIs, loading/error states as first-class UX, optimistic updates, and race conditions when requests overlap (stale responses arriving late). SWR/React-Query patterns formalize caching and revalidation. Every 'the app feels fast' trick is here.
notes.focus: Break your app deliberately: fire two overlapping requests and render the stale one. Then fix it with cancellation — race bugs you've SEEN are race bugs you'll never ship.

notes.summary: Quality at web scale: unit tests for logic, integration tests for API routes, and end-to-end browser tests (Playwright — the same tool family this study app was verified with). The testing pyramid, fixture design, and making async code testable. Your 61A/61B testing discipline scales up unchanged.
notes.focus: Write a Playwright test that logs into a real app and asserts one behavior. That single E2E test guards more regressions than twenty unit tests.

notes.summary: Architecture under load: the request path through CDN, load balancer, app tier, and database; caching at every layer (HTTP, Redis, memoization); horizontal scaling and statelessness. Your 6.829 (CDNs, queueing) and 6.830 (indexes, replication) courses supply the theory — this lecture deploys it.
notes.focus: Estimate: requests/sec for 1M daily users, then the machines needed at given latency budgets. The arithmetic IS capacity planning.

notes.summary: Shipping as a discipline: build pipelines, environment configuration (the 12-factor rules), containerization basics, and observability — logs, metrics, and error budgets. Full Stack Ocean deploys on Render with exactly this pipeline; studying its deploys makes the abstraction concrete.
notes.focus: Write the deploy checklist for a web app: build, migrate, health-check, release, rollback trigger. The checklist is the difference between deploying and praying.

lessons.title: Modern Web: TypeScript and the Ecosystem

notes.summary: The professional layer: TypeScript's types for large codebases (your 6.100L static-typing lesson, webbed), bundlers and the module graph, SSR vs SPA trade-offs, and the framework ecosystem's design space. Where CS50's Flask ended, this lecture makes you fluent in how real teams build.
notes.focus: Convert one JS module to TypeScript and let the types find one latent bug. That moment justifies the entire type system in production.

notes.summary: The presentation layer done properly: the box model, flexbox and grid as layout systems, media queries and responsive breakpoints, and accessibility as a design constraint rather than an afterthought. Full Stack Ocean's espresso-and-champagne design system (glass, shadows, type scale) is a worked example — inspect it while you study.
notes.focus: Recreate a layout from a screenshot using grid only, then flexbox only. Fluency in both is what makes UI work fast — and fun.

notes.summary: Checkpoint: your React client, Node server, and database working as one system with real auth. The midterm for a builder's course is the integration itself — every layer exercised end to end. Test every path a user can take, then fix what you find.
notes.focus: Have someone else USE your app for ten minutes while you watch silently. Every hesitation they make is your real midterm feedback.

notes.summary: The final: a deployed, tested, documented application of your own design — the course's answer to 'can you build software people can use?' Every course in the path contributed: languages, algorithms, systems, databases, security, and now delivery. This artifact (with the capstone project) becomes your professional portfolio's centerpiece.
notes.focus: Polish one feature until it delights instead of shipping five that merely work. Demo day rewards focus — and so does every code review for the rest of your career.
